title: US Hedge Funds Just Sold Every AI Stock They Bought Since 2025
content:
For five straight days in October, hedge funds sold AI stocks. By the end, they had undone every AI purchase they made since the start of 2025, Goldman Sachs data shows.
Morgan Stanley says hedge funds have cut more than 8% of their total stock bets since June, their biggest retreat since at least 2017. The pain showed on stock prices, as big tech stocks crashed last week and erased $2 trillion from the market.
The pain landed in one corner of the market. The S&P 500 barely moved through late October. Memory chipmakers Samsung, SK Hynix, Micron, and SanDisk lost more than $700 billion in under two weeks.
Why Hedge Funds Ran From AI Stocks
Hedge funds borrow to make their bets bigger. When prices fall, losses grow fast, so funds sell to cut risk. That selling drags prices lower and forces more selling.
Most were running for the exit, not betting on a crash. On the heaviest day, they sold shares they owned about 3.5 times faster than they opened new bets against stocks, according to Goldman figures.
Then came October 22. Goldman's basket of hedge funds' favorite stocks fell 4.2%, its worst day since 2011. The bank's prime desk summed it up.
      "If last Thursday felt bad, today has been worse,"
Is the AI Bubble Bursting, or Are Funds Just Selling?
Macro investor Jordi Visser blames borrowed money, not weak demand. He estimated the leverage took 18 months to build and 75 days to unwind.
Corporate profits are up about 20%, and AI computing demand still outruns supply. SK Hynix forecasts a memory shortage until 2030. Fundstrat's Tom Lee suspects one forced seller drove the slide.
Goldman sees a darker picture. The bank said the unwind looks closer to its start than its end, Deep News reported. Funds' AI holdings still rank in the top 17% of the past three years.
On October 26, BeInCrypto asked whether China's AI bubble burst would reach America. Days later, a late-October selloff wiped about $2 trillion off the Nasdaq-100.
If Goldman is right, hedge funds still have plenty left to sell.

report.summary: Hedge funds unwound every AI stock position added since early 2025 in a five-day October selloff, wiping $2 trillion in market value and reviving bubble questions.
report.background: Since ChatGPT's launch, AI has been the dominant equity trade of 2023-2025, with capital crowding into Nvidia, hyperscalers, and especially memory makers riding HBM and DRAM demand. Hedge funds amplified the trade using prime-brokerage leverage, so AI names became both the market's biggest profit engine and its most crowded position. Through mid-2025, positioning hit extremes: Goldman Sachs' VIP basket of fund favorites traded near record concentration, and memory chipmakers in Korea and the US absorbed outsized flows as AI datacenter buildouts strained supply. When momentum stalled in October, margin mechanics took over. Forced de-grossing, not a change in AI demand, drove the cascade. The episode echoes prior crowded-trade blowups and highlights how much of the AI narrative is now mediated by leveraged financial flows rather than end-user adoption.
key_points: Five straight days of selling in October erased every AI stock purchase hedge funds made since January 2025, according to Goldman Sachs prime brokerage data. The retreat was defensive de-risking, not a directional short bet: on the heaviest day, funds sold long positions about 3.5 times faster than they opened new shorts.

Morgan Stanley says hedge funds cut more than 8% of total equity exposure since June, their largest pullback since at least 2017. The pain was concentrated: the S&P 500 barely moved through late October while Goldman's basket of fund favorites fell 4.2% in one day, its worst since 2011.

Memory chips absorbed the sharpest blow. Samsung, SK Hynix, Micron, and SanDisk shed more than $700 billion in under two weeks as AI hardware bets unwound. Big tech's slide erased roughly $2 trillion from markets, and the Nasdaq-100 took another $2 trillion hit days later.

Investors disagree on the cause. Jordi Visser blames leverage, estimating it took 18 months to build and 75 days to unwind, while Fundstrat's Tom Lee suspects a single forced seller. Fundamentals look intact: corporate profits are up about 20% and SK Hynix forecasts memory shortages until 2030.

Goldman is more bearish, saying the unwind looks closer to its start than its end. Funds' AI holdings still sit in the top 17% of the past three years, meaning substantial exposure remains available to sell if prices keep falling — a setup for further cascading pressure.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the selloff is a financing signal more than a demand signal. Model builders and datacenter operators still face supply-constrained compute, but startups dependent on equity markets for capital may find funding rounds slower and valuations compressed. For developers, the practical effect is indirect: cloud pricing and GPU availability are unlikely to improve quickly, though a market reset could cool speculative infrastructure spending and force more efficient tooling. For regular users, AI products keep shipping, but the era of frictionless, cheap capital behind them is narrowing. The deeper lesson is structural: AI stocks now behave like a leveraged macro trade, so headlines about model releases increasingly compete with margin calls and prime-brokerage flows in setting prices.
